headline: High: Flowise can write shared files while Copilot reads repo/editor context, creating default-path prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Flowise can write to the server filesystem and ingest uploaded files; Copilot reads repo context and editor buffers. If Flowise outputs attacker-controlled content into a shared workspace, Copilot may treat it as trusted context. This is not proven by a documented direct bridge, so I rate it medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Flowise writes untrusted content into a directory Copilot indexes
IF Copilot is asked to summarize or act on that content without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate Flowise output directories from Copilot-opened repos
Mark Flowise-generated files with a clear prefix or folder
Review Copilot prompts before accepting generated edits
Disable automatic indexing of Flowise output folders
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs and uploaded files, while Copilot reads repo context and open buffers and sends requests to api.githubcopilot.com. A shared workspace can move sensitive content from Flowise into Copilot’s cloud-backed context. The profiles do not prove a default shared filesystem, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents access the same project directory or uploaded artifacts
IF sensitive chatflow inputs are present in files Copilot can read
mitigations: Keep sensitive Flowise artifacts outside Copilot-visible repos
Use separate OS accounts or workspaces
Remove secrets from uploaded files before reuse
Turn off Copilot on directories containing sensitive Flowise outputs
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files, and Flowise has server-filesystem access while Copilot can modify editor buffers and Workspace edits. That creates overlapping writes to shared mutable resources, though the profiles do not show unrestricted same-dir writes or git locking issues. Uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF Flowise and Copilot target the same directory or file set
IF Copilot Workspace applies edits while Flowise writes generated artifacts
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate output directory
Avoid simultaneous edits to the same files
Use git branches for one agent at a time
Check diffs before merging agent output
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transaction semantics

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise produces graph-based tool outputs, and Copilot Workspace/chat can turn repo context into edits. If Copilot treats Flowise-generated text or files as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect code changes or actions. The profiles show a plausible handoff but not a guaranteed verification gap, so medium fits.
conditions: IF Copilot consumes Flowise-generated files as source material
IF no human or automated verification step checks Flowise outputs before edits
mitigations: Require human review of Flowise outputs before Copilot uses them
Add a validation step for generated files
Keep Flowise outputs read-only until reviewed
Use tests or linters before accepting Copilot edits
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and touch general code/chatflow data, but neither profile states a residency, certification, or retention mismatch. Copilot has GitHub repo OAuth context while Flowise handles model keys and tool credentials, so compliance risk exists only if regulated data is placed into the shared workflow. The other agent is not separately cited because no mismatch is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into Flowise chatflows or Copilot buffers
IF organizational policy forbids GitHub-hosted context for that data class
mitigations: Do not place regulated data in shared prompts or files
Use a policy check before enabling either agent on sensitive projects
Store secrets in approved secret managers only
Review retention settings for both tools
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
